Our master Rabbi Bunim said that on this it is written, ‘Do not say that the former days were better than these’, for then the awakening was very strong: ‘for it is not out of wisdom that you ask this’, that is, it was not from your own wisdom, only as a loan (she’elah) from Hashem, and the essential thing is what one acquires afterward through his toil. And our holy master of Izhbitz said: whatever a person has the power to attain later as a possession, Hashem shows to him at the beginning as a seeing, and it is only on loan; afterward it departs, so that he will toil afterward to attain it as a possession.”

k: volume-i|1900|0|R. Shmuel Bornsztain, Shem MiShmuel, Pes
quote: Parallel: R. Shmuel Bornsztain, Shem MiShmuel, Pesach 15:5-11: “‘Hashem will fight for you and you shall be silent.’ In the holy Zohar: ‘Be silent, certainly, and do not awaken a word ... and therefore this judgment was in mercy; and so the Holy One, blessed be He, did not want Israel to awaken a word, for if Israel awakened a word, the Name of Mercy would not be awakened and judgment would not be done in mercy.’ ... When Hashem gives to Israel from kindness alone, the nations come with the claim that they too need kindness, and how do these differ from those? ... In truth, although everything was in kindness and mercy, the matter depending on Atika, where there is no admixture of judgment, there is still a judgment as to who is fit to receive the kindness; and therefore Israel, who gave over their lives and entered the sea up to their nostrils, were the ones fit to receive it. ... Now the words of the Zohar are understood, that Israel had not to awaken, for if Israel awakened there would be judgment without mercy: for this is the measure, that the Holy One answers all who call upon Him in truth, and then the Egyptians would no longer be so foolish as to pursue, since Israel would be the ones bringing about the splitting of the sea by the merit of their prayer.”

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Pesach 35:2: “Afterward the holy Zohar says: ‘Come and see: here, when Pharaoh drew near ... the Holy One, blessed be He, did not want Israel to awaken any awakening below at all ... be silent, certainly.’ One must understand why he opened with the verse about Shabbat when the whole subject is the splitting of the Red Sea. But in truth the splitting of the sea depended on Atika, as the holy Zohar says, ‘to Me precisely: everything depends on Atika’; and on Shabbat too there is a revelation of Atika. Here he teaches that there is a difference: on Shabbat, although there is a revelation of Atika and the essence of the holiness comes from Hashem, there must nevertheless be an awakening from below on man's part, as it says ‘and you shall call,’ meaning that he invites it, for preparation is needed on man's part. Not so at the splitting of the sea, when there was the accusation ‘How do these differ from those?’ as stated in the Midrash and the holy Zohar. Therefore he said, ‘Hashem will fight for you and you shall be silent,’ certainly, and do not awaken a word; for if there were an awakening from below, there would be an accusation as to whether they were worthy of it. ... The essence depended on Atika, and that is the merit of Avraham, who merited the attribute of ‘elder’; and the Midrash mentions the merit of Yaakov, who is the river that goes out from Eden, which is a drawing down of the light of Atika.”

Parallel: Maharal, Derashat Shabbat HaGadol 10:11-13: “Rava, or some say R. Yochanan, said: The world endures only for the sake of Moshe and Aharon; it is written here, ‘And what (mah) are we,’ and it is written there, ‘He hangs the earth upon belimah.’ The explanation is that the earth is the foundation of everything and bears everything, for creatures walk upon the earth and all is upon it, because earth is the lowest and humblest of the elements; therefore the earth has greater permanence from Hashem, who upholds the lowly more than all because of their lowliness. Yet the earth, though lowest of all, is still reckoned as something, and one cannot say of it that it is nothing at all. Therefore he said that this earth stands upon one who is ‘what,’ meaning one who likens himself to nothing, as Moshe and Aharon were ‘what’ in their own eyes and regarded themselves as though they were nothing; upon these the earth stands. ... Moshe said, ‘What am I, that the Torah should be given through me?’ and made himself small until he was like ‘what’ ... and the Torah was fitting for him because he made himself ‘what’; if so, he is not bounded at all, and he can receive the Torah even though it is broader than the world.”

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Ki Teitzei 15:2: “What is called ‘a halachah to Moshe from Sinai’ is along the lines of what is said in Tosafot Chadashim on ‘Moshe received the Torah from Sinai’: that he merited to have the Torah given through him was ‘from Sinai,’ because of his great humility, the very reason Mount Sinai merited that the Torah be given upon it, as they expounded (Megillah 29a) on the verse ‘Why do you look askance, you peaked mountains’: all of you are blemished compared with Sinai. ... Therefore, because Moshe was humbler than any man, he merited wisdom from Ayin, from the attribute of the Infinite, as it is said, ‘And wisdom, from where (me-ayin) shall it be found?’ So the holy Zohar says in Beshalach on the verse ‘Is Hashem among us or not (ayin)?’ ... Atika Setima’ah, which is called Ayin. And in Sotah (21b): in one who makes himself as though he is not; that is, he becomes a chariot for the attribute of Ayin, which is Atika, the aspect of the Infinite. And this only Moshe our teacher merited, who said ‘And what are we,’ as is taught (Chullin 89a): Greater is what is said of Moshe and Aharon than what is said of Avraham, for of Avraham it is written, ‘I am dust and ashes,’ which is still some substance, while of Moshe it is written, ‘And what are we,’ that is, like one who is not.”

k: volume-i|1904|0|R. Yehudah Aryeh Leib Alter, Sefat Emet,
quote: Parallel: R. Yehudah Aryeh Leib Alter, Sefat Emet, Bamidbar 17:2: “It is possible that these are the three Shabbatot we find: at Marah, at Sinai, and in the work of the Mishkan; for there is an aspect of Shabbat in receiving an additional nefesh, ruach and neshamah. That is, in ceasing from one’s works, at Marah and in the section of the manna, ‘and they shall prepare what they bring ... and they rested’: this is the aspect of ‘Observe’ (shamor), for the aspect of nefesh needs guarding; therefore it is written there, ‘as Hashem your God commanded you’ (at Marah). And ‘Remember’ is with the mouth, the sanctification of the day, the receiving of the ruach. And at the Mishkan it is written, ‘It is a sign between Me and you ... to know,’ and the Sages expounded: in private, for the aspect of the additional neshamah was not revealed. ... This may be the intent of the Sages’ saying: had Israel kept the first Shabbat, no nation would have ruled over them, for it is written ... ‘and Amalek came.’ Tosafot asked why it is called the ‘first Shabbat’; according to what we have said it is well, for it is the first level of Shabbat, ‘Observe,’ which requires guarding. There Israel stumbled, and there Amalek had the power to touch them; yet afterward they repaired it, and after they weakened Amalek it is written, ‘And the people rested on the seventh day.’”

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Bechukosai 1:2: “Shabbat is also called ‘statute’ (chok), as stated in the Mekhilta, ‘statute: this is Shabbat’; that is, on Shabbat one merits the Oral Torah being engraved (nechkak) in the heart without toil. For it is taught in the Yerushalmi: Shabbatot were given only for eating and drinking; and others say: Shabbatot were given only to engage in words of Torah. And it is taught in the Pesikta that they do not disagree: the one who says for Torah study speaks of laborers, and the one who says for delight speaks of Torah scholars. ... Even to engage in Torah, one nevertheless merits on Shabbat Torah without toil, engraved in the heart. ... And at Marah, when their soul was bitter because the illumination they had at the Sea had departed from them, ‘there He made for them a statute’: this is Shabbat, so that through Shabbat they would be assured that it would be engraved in the heart and they would not falter again. ... This is what we say on Motzaei Shabbat in the Havdalah of the Amidah, ‘You have favored us with knowledge of Your Torah’: that is, the Oral Torah, which is the Holy Spirit, as the Ramban wrote (Bava Batra 12a), and this is called da’at ... ‘And You taught us to perform the statutes of Your will’: that is Shabbat, which is called ‘statute,’ for words of Torah are engraved in the heart.”

k: volume-i|1906|0|Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Chodesh Adar II 1:1
ref: Peri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Adar II 1:1
quote: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Chodesh Adar II 1:1: “The Sages said (Bereshit Rabbah 17): The beginning of a fall is sleep: he dozes and does not toil in Torah. And so it says, ‘Laziness casts into a deep sleep’; and they said, ‘Rephidim’ means only that they slackened their hands from the Torah, and therefore Amalek came upon them. Amalek is the root of the evil inclination, as stated in the Zohar (III 160a): ‘Amalek ... this is the evil inclination, the accuser and prosecutor of man’; and he casts slackness of the hands from Torah, ‘laziness casts into a deep sleep.’ And it is written, ‘who cooled you (asher karcha),’ for he casts coldness upon a person and laziness from toiling in Torah, and this is the first of the kelipah. Likewise there is a Gehinnom of fire corresponding to lust, the incitement of the serpent ... and there is a Gehinnom of snow corresponding to the coldness, the root of the kelipah, ‘first of the nations, Amalek,’ ‘who cooled you.’ ... And regarding blotting out Amalek it is written, ‘when Hashem gives you rest from all your enemies round about’: that is, when one merits to repair the root of the evil inclination and to have rest from all the accusations of the evil inclination, which is called simply ‘enemy.’”

k: volume-i|1907|0|R. Shneur Zalman of Liadi, Tanya, Likkut
quote: Parallel: R. Shneur Zalman of Liadi, Tanya, Likkutei Amarim 42:1-3: “What has been explained about the lower fear makes clear what the Gemara says on the verse, ‘And now, Israel, what does Hashem your God ask of you but to fear Hashem your God’: Is fear a small thing? Yes, for Moshe it is a small thing. ... The matter is that every soul of the house of Israel contains something of Moshe our teacher, for he is one of the seven shepherds who draw vitality and Godliness to the totality of Israel's souls, which is why they are called shepherds. Moshe our teacher is the sum of them all and is called the ‘faithful shepherd,’ for he draws the faculty of da’at to the whole of Israel, to know Hashem, each according to the grasp of his soul and its root above, and its nourishment from the root of the soul of Moshe our teacher, which is rooted in the supernal Da’at. ... Moreover, in every generation sparks of the soul of Moshe our teacher descend and clothe themselves in the body and soul of the sages of the generation, ‘the eyes of the congregation,’ to teach the people knowledge, to know the greatness of Hashem and to serve Him with heart and soul; for the service of the heart is according to the da’at, as it is written, ‘Know the God of your father and serve Him with a whole heart and a willing soul.’”

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Kedoshim 14:1: “Even though tzitzit is a guard against the evil inclination ... nevertheless the evil inclination can entice a person, blind his eyes and call evil good; of this the Gemara says that the evil inclination sits between the two entrances of the heart: sometimes the evil inclination sits on the wise heart at his right and makes itself out to be enticing him toward a good path. Even with our father Yaakov we find (Chullin 91a) that he appeared to him like a Torah scholar and attached himself to his right, making himself out to be guiding him for good; but Yaakov sensed at once that it was not so, and he could not prevail over him, whereas another person he can turn aside. ... Yaakov merited this by recognizing that all that He did was for good, from Hashem, as he said, ‘the God who has shepherded me all my life’; and through this the Holy One guarded him in all his deeds, even beyond human understanding. So too King David said, ‘Hashem is my shepherd, I shall not lack ... He leads me in paths of righteousness,’ that everything is from Hashem; accordingly he said of the incident that befell him that it never occurred to him that he was committing a sin, as stated (Sanhedrin 107a): Bat Sheva was fitting for David from the six days of creation. And after he heard from the prophet, ‘You are the man,’ he said, ‘Even though I walk in the valley of the shadow of death I will fear no evil, for You are with me’: certainly You guard me beyond my grasp,

Parallel: Takanas HaShavin 10:1: “The first: repentance from love, and through it one rectifies what came before; see Yoma 86b, that through repentance from love willful sins become like merits. If so, Rashi's explanation on ‘from the outset shovavim,’ as though the beginning of the sin came through youthfulness, seemingly requires study. It appears that ‘from the outset shovavim’ means before the repentance: for through repentance from love it becomes clear that even at the time of the sin, before the repentance, he did not do it from his heart at all, but only as an act of youth and mere folly, as they said (Sotah 3a): a person does not commit a transgression unless a spirit of folly enters him. There they said it as a general rule about every Jew, because in truth all Israel's hearts are turned to Heaven ... and as stated in Berakhot 17a: ‘It is revealed and known before You that our will is to do Your will; and what prevents it? The leaven in the dough.’ ... In this world, one who merits to return out of love merits this, for it becomes clear that even before, at the time of the sin, it was only waywardness and an act of youth and not complete willfulness, and through this, after the repentance, it becomes like merits.”

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Bechukotai 10:2: “And afterward it is written, ‘And I will give peace in the land.’ The essence of peace is peace from the accusation of the evil inclination, as it says, ‘There is no peace in my bones because of my sin’, and this is the essential perpetual war with the evil inclination. … As is said in the name of our master Rabbi Bunim, that the explanation of ‘When you go out to war against your enemy’ as referring to the evil inclination is not a matter of derash and hint but the plain meaning, for the war of the inclination is the main war, and it is constant. And it is stated in the Sifrei (Ekev): ‘You shall eat and be satisfied; beware lest your heart be enticed’, for a person rebels against the Holy One only out of satiety. … So too all eating can lead to sin, as it says (Bava Batra 12b), after one eats and drinks he has only one heart. That is: if it is not in holiness, it will be only the heart of the fool on his left; and when it is in holiness, it will bring only the heart of the wise on his right. … Then eating will not bring to the evil inclination; on the contrary, the eating will cause words of Torah and holiness to come into the heart, for eating that Hashem gives is ‘Come, eat of My bread and drink of the wine I have mixed’, which is words of Torah. This is what Jacob our father asked: ‘and He will give me bread to eat’.”

k: volume-i|1911|0|R. Yehudah Aryeh Leib Alter, Sefat Emet,
quote: Parallel: R. Yehudah Aryeh Leib Alter, Sefat Emet, Beshalach 5656: “On the portion of the manna: ‘Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you … that I may test them.’ For according to a person’s food, so does he merit Torah, according to the holiness of the food. This is what the Sages said: the Torah was given only to those who ate the manna, and second to them those who eat terumah, for terumah too is called holy. In truth, even ordinary food that has been rectified, from which terumah and tithes were taken, retains an imprint of holiness; and therefore there is no Torah like the Torah of the Land of Israel, because the food and sustenance is rectified through the commandments that depend on the Land. Now, because of our sins, all this is lacking to us; and therefore on the holy Sabbath, which is the meal of faith, we merit more Torah. Had it not been for the sin of the Calf, they would have been nourished from the bread of the manna, as it says, ‘I said, you are godlike beings’. … And the generation of the wilderness, who merited to hear the word of Hashem at Mount Sinai, were given in the same way a food that the ministering angels eat.”

k: volume-i|1912|0|R. Moshe Chaim Ephraim of Sudilkov, Dege
quote: Parallel: R. Moshe Chaim Ephraim of Sudilkov, Degel Machaneh Ephraim, Eikev 4: “I heard from my master [the Baal Shem Tov] on the matter of ‘no fly was seen on his table’: according to the refinement of a person’s thought, so the worlds rest upon him, and so do matters pass before him in what he sees and hears. … Holiness is called Wisdom, as explained in the holy Zohar that Chokhmah is called holy; and I wrote in the name of my master and grandfather that wisdom is called ‘the graves of lust’, for when a person comes to wisdom, all foreign physical desires cease from him, except what is needed to sustain a person in this world. … One who cleaves to wisdom cleaves to goodness and kindness. ‘Good’ (tov) has the numerical value seventeen, as is known, and ‘fly’ (zevuv) is also seventeen, and it is the aspect of the husks opposite the aspect of good. … And this is what is alluded to in ‘dead flies make the perfumer’s oil putrid’ … Therefore, when the Shunammite saw that no fly was seen on his pure table, she understood that he surely cleaves to goodness, kindness and wisdom. This is what she said, ‘a holy man’, meaning one who cleaves to wisdom, which is holiness, and nullifies all physical desires; and consequently no pollution was seen on his sheets, since he cleaves to wisdom and life.”

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Ki Tisa 1:1: “The essential thing is to rectify the blemish of the serpent, which began with its enticement in eating, and afterward it cast defilement into Eve (Shabbat 146a), and the defilement clung to her seed. At the Giving of the Torah Israel’s defilement ceased (as stated there), and then they rectified the whole blemish of the serpent. … And the essential rectification of the blemish is through words of Torah, which is a rectification for the future, as is stated (Zohar I 202a): ‘for there is nothing to break the evil inclination but the Torah’, and likewise to rectify the past, as it is written, ‘and healing to all his flesh’. … The tribe of Levi will rectify the blemish through eating in holiness, eating terumah, which is called holy (Moed Katan 28a), and they made the eating of terumah outside the Temple like the service of the Temple (Pesachim 73a). Every descendant of Levi and Aaron merits this even if he is not a Torah scholar, since he eats in holiness and rectifies the blemish of the serpent, though the essential rectification is through words of Torah. … And of the tribe of Shimon he said, ‘I will scatter them in Israel’: they will rectify the blemish by bringing words of Torah into the hearts of schoolchildren.”

k: volume-i|1914|0|R. Kalonymus Kalman Epstein, Maor VaShem
quote: Parallel: R. Kalonymus Kalman Epstein, Maor VaShemesh, Beshalach 1: “The early commentators already raised this: why at first is ‘the people’ said without qualification, and afterward ‘and the children of Israel went up armed’? It should have used one expression in both. … The Holy One foresaw that if they came immediately to the Land of Israel with the Mixed Multitude among them, many evil stumbling-blocks would sprout for Israel, Heaven forbid. Therefore He led them round by way of the wilderness of the Red Sea; perhaps when they saw that the wilderness had closed upon them, and Pharaoh and his army pursuing with chariots and horsemen, and also saw the war of Amalek, they would take it to heart to turn back, and all the workers of iniquity would be separated. It is known from the books that wherever ‘the people’ is said without qualification it means the Mixed Multitude. … And the verse concludes, ‘and the children of Israel went up armed (chamushim) from the land of Egypt’: that is, not so the children of Israel; they were ready for the service of their Creator and cleaved to the World of Repentance. This is ‘and the children of Israel went up chamushim’: they cleaved to the gate of Nun (fifty), which is the World of Repentance, and they repented in truth.”

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Vaera 10:3–4: “It is stated (Tikkunei Zohar, Tikkun 6): from the Throne are the neshamot, from the Chayah the ruchin, and from the Ophan the nefashot, and they are in Beriah, Yetzirah and Asiyah. That is: the nefesh is from Asiyah, from the final Hei, ‘and He rested (vayinafash)’, from where the nefashot fly forth, and the nefesh is mostly evil. The ruach is from Yetzirah, and it is in the heart, which has two chambers, ‘the heart of the wise at his right and the heart of the fool at his left’, and it is half good and half evil. And from the Throne come the neshamot, from Beriah, where it is mostly good, as it is written, ‘the soul You gave within me is pure.’ The four letters of Havayah correspond to the four worlds Atzilut, Beriah, Yetzirah, Asiyah: the lower Hei is the world of Asiyah; the Vav the world of Yetzirah; the upper Hei Beriah; the Yod the world of Atzilut, and from there is the soul of the soul, which divides into two levels, Chayah and Yechidah, corresponding to the Yod and the tag of the Yod that alludes to Keter Elyon, and there it is entirely good, as is known.”

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Pesach 7:1: “And He reckoned ‘He brought us out from slavery to freedom’, the world of freedom, Binah, for the Exodus from Egypt was from the side of the Jubilee, as stated in the holy Zohar on the verse ‘and the children of Israel went up chamushim’. … And the five expressions correspond to the five levels in the soul, nefesh, ruach, neshamah, chayah, yechidah (Midrash Rabbah, end of Va’etchanan), and they correspond to the four letters of Havayah and the tag of the Yod, which alludes to Keter Elyon (Zohar III 65b). … And the five expressions, each of them comprising ten, are the fifty gates of Binah. And the ten plagues, which were a smiting to Egypt and a healing to Israel, of which Rabbi Akiva said that each one comprised five, correspond to the five powers of the soul, which come from the four letters of Havayah and the tag of the Yod, five partzufim; so they were struck with fifty plagues. And at the Splitting of the Sea, even according to Rabbi Yose HaGelili, they were struck with fifty plagues. All of this corresponds to the five partzufim, the five times ‘Bless, O my soul’ in the Gemara (Berakhot 10a), and the five levels of the soul. And the Exodus from Egypt came about through their meriting the fifty gates of Binah, as it is written, ‘and the children of Israel went up chamushim’.”

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Pesach 38:1: “The root of the exiles is to rectify the blemish of the covenant, the sin of the generation of the Flood … and the first exile was in Egypt, ‘the nakedness of the land’, so that Israel be clarified in the attribute of Tzaddik. It is brought in the writings of the Ari that the very souls that were in the Flood were in Egypt, and the decree ‘into the river you shall cast him’ came upon them. … It is stated in the holy Zohar (Beshalach 49a): What did the sea see? It saw the coffin of Joseph and fled before it, because it is written of him ‘and he fled and went outside’, and so ‘the sea saw and fled’ (and so in Bereshit Rabbah 87). The matter is that all Israel are called by the name of Joseph, ‘the remnant of Joseph’ (Bereshit Rabbah 71), for Joseph clarifies all Israel, ‘and your people are all righteous’, since whoever is circumcised is called righteous; for although each tribe had its own holiness, its holiness was included in all the tribes, as it says, ‘each according to his blessing he blessed them’. … And because at the Splitting of the Sea there were still claims against Israel in this matter, it says, ‘and Hashem drove the sea with a strong east wind all night’; through this a spirit of purity blew into the hearts of Israel to purify them from the desires called ‘the raging waters’, ‘and He made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided’, and through this afterward, of itself, ‘the sea saw and fled’, for it saw the coffin of Jose

k: volume-i|1918|0|R. Dov Ber of Mezeritch, Maggid Devarav
quote: Parallel: R. Dov Ber of Mezeritch, Maggid Devarav LeYaakov 119: “It is said in the Midrash: ‘to Him who cut the Red Sea into parts (gezarim)’, into circumcised ones (gezurin), which is the eight days of circumcision. This is understood from what the Sages said: ‘The sea saw and fled’; what did it see? It saw the coffin of Joseph. And in the Zohar it is explained: it saw ‘and he fled and went outside’. The meaning is that the tzaddik sifts the good from the evil. … So it was with Joseph the tzaddik: she enticed him with words and with garments she wore for him in the morning, and she was beautiful and adorned herself before him; and when he saw her, he sifted the good from her and attached his thought to the Tiferet of Israel above, and this is what the Sages said, that he saw the image of his father. This is ‘and he fled and went outside’, and it does not say ‘outside’ alone, meaning that he fled and went out beyond the material world and cleaved to the upper world. And his merit caused that ‘the sea saw’ his coffin ‘and fled’, also beyond this world into the upper world, where there is no water, … and of itself it became dry land; and all this in the merit of the tzaddik who guards the covenant. This is ‘to Him who cut the Red Sea into parts’, meaning into circumcised ones.”

k: volume-i|1919|0|R. Shneur Zalman of Liadi, Tanya, Iggere
quote: Parallel: R. Shneur Zalman of Liadi, Tanya, Iggeret HaTeshuvah 9: “This is the cleaving of spirit to spirit in the utmost attachment and union, when it comes from love. And since the blemish of the covenant through wasteful emission, and all the more so through forbidden unions, whether Torah prohibitions or rabbinic ones, for the words of the Scribes are weightier, makes a blemish in the brain, therefore its rectification is that he occupy himself with Torah, which issues from Chokhmah. This is what is said in Tanna DeVei Eliyahu: A man committed a transgression and became liable to death before the Omnipresent; what shall he do and live? If he was accustomed to read one page, let him read two; to learn one chapter, let him learn two chapters. It is like a cord that was cut and tied again, where at the place of the knot it is doubled and redoubled; and so it is with “the cord of His inheritance.” This is the meaning of the verse, “Through kindness and truth iniquity is atoned,” and there is no truth but Torah; and the sin of the house of Eli is not atoned through sacrifice and offering, but it is atoned through Torah and acts of kindness, as stated at the end of the first chapter of Rosh Hashanah.”

k: volume-i|1920|0|Pri Tzaddik, Vayeilech and Shabbat Shuva
ref: Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbat Shuvah 9:1
quote: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Vayeilech and Shabbat Shuvah 9:1: “The prophet said, ‘Take words with you,’ at least words alone. He is not speaking of one whose mouth and heart are not alike, Heaven forbid, but of one who for the moment truly wishes to return, even though afterward his inclination overpowers him; nevertheless, at the time of the act he is called a penitent. As we said from what is taught (Kiddushin 49b): one who betroths a woman ‘on condition that I am righteous,’ even if he is a complete rasha she is betrothed, lest he had a thought of repentance. This implies that we see him still conducting himself in his wickedness, for otherwise he has certainly turned from his evil. If so, how can it say ‘lest he had a thought of repentance’ and he is righteous? The definition of repentance is until the Knower of secrets testifies about him that he will never return to this sin, as the Rambam wrote. But since at that moment it was in his mind to abandon his wickedness and return, even though his inclination overpowered him afterward and he went back to his ways, nevertheless in that moment he is called a tzaddik. ... Afterward we pray, ‘Bring us back in complete repentance,’ that the evil inclination be uprooted and the repentance be complete, until the Knower of secrets testifies about him that he will truly never return to this sin; and this comes only through Hashem’s help. And on Shabbat ... we say the song ‘It is good to give thanks (lehodos) to Hashem’: he confesses, with

k: volume-i|1921|0|R. Kalonymus Kalman Epstein, Maor VaShem
quote: Parallel: R. Kalonymus Kalman Epstein, Maor VaShemesh, Beshalach 8: “Through the awakening from below one raises the feminine waters up to Malchut, and Malchut raises them to the world above it, and so from world to world up to Binah; but from Binah upward no human being has the power to raise the feminine waters, and there the union must come from Him and through Him, that is, Binah raises the waters to the world above it, and so from world to world up to Atika, and the masculine waters are revealed, and through this wonders and miracles are worked for Israel. To awaken the secret of Atika is impossible for man. ... At the splitting of the Red Sea there was an accusation against Israel ... and the secret of Atika had to be awakened so that the severities would be sweetened at their root and great kindness and simple mercy would flow upon them, so that the sea would split before them. When Israel saw the sea closed before them and Pharaoh pursuing them, they took up the craft of their fathers and cried out to Hashem; but through their prayer it was impossible for the sea to split before them, since through the awakening from below the waters rise only up to Binah. ... This is the meaning of ‘Why do you cry out to Me’: ‘It is not the time for prayer,’ that is, now is not the time to pray, for the splitting of the sea will not be effected through prayer; ‘to Me’ precisely, meaning this union depends on Me, ‘it depends on Atika.’ And this is what Moshe said to Israel, ‘Hashem wi

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Pekudei 9:1: “‘And you shall call the Sabbath a delight ... then (az) you shall delight upon Hashem’: that is, one merits the revelation of the dimension of Atika, which is called ‘upon Hashem,’ as the holy Zohar says (Yitro 83a): what is ‘upon Hashem’? ... as it is written, ‘From where (me-ayin) will my help come,’ and it is written, ‘He came to the Ancient of Days.’ That is, it is above the Name Havayah, which denotes the nine attributes ... and the cusp of the upper Yod alludes to Ayin; and this is ‘upon Hashem.’ And this is the secret of ‘Az’: the Alef, the supernal Pele, that reaches to the Zayin. And on Shabbat there is a revelation of Atika, as the holy Zohar says; and about this it says, ‘Then (az) you shall call and Hashem will answer,’ also with ‘az.’ This is according to what is taught (Shabbat 118b): whoever delights in the Sabbath is granted the petitions of his heart. And in truth, through the mitzvah of tzedakah too one merits the light of Atika ... and the terms ‘ram’ and ‘terum’ (lifted, exalted) denote what is above grasp, which is the dimension of Atika.”

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Vaera 6:1: “‘Rejoice, reapers of the field, with speech and with voice.’ ... The reapers of the field come only through the tzaddik, the gardener of the garden; and a tzaddik is called a mighty one who conquers his inclination, who did not spoil. And if he spoiled, what will become of him? About this he said ‘with speech and with voice,’ which is the rectification for this. ‘Speech’ means words of Torah ... and ‘with voice’ means prayer, for the essence of prayer is crying out, which is a voice without speech, as the holy Zohar says ... And on Shabbat, when there is no crying out, we nevertheless pray, ‘Grant our portion in Your Torah,’ for this is the essence of prayer on Shabbat, as is taught (Berakhot 29a): these seven blessings of Shabbat correspond to the seven voices that David spoke over the waters. And there is no water other than Torah, and they correspond to the seven voices of the Giving of the Torah: the Torah was given with five voices, and it is written, ‘And all the people saw the voices,’ two more voices. And although we say (Berakhot 6b) that those voices were before the Giving of the Torah, the meaning is that they remained forever, for from them the awe remained, as it says, ‘so that His fear may be upon your faces, that you not sin.’ Those voices remained forever, for ‘saw’ (ro’im) is written in the present tense.”

k: volume-i|1924|0|R. Menachem Nachum of Chernobyl, Me'or E
quote: Parallel: R. Menachem Nachum of Chernobyl, Me'or Einayim, Devarim 5: “Through the holiness of Shabbat da’at is drawn into every person who wishes to bind himself to the Creator, blessed be He, for on Shabbat there is an abundance of da’at, with expanded mind and great delight, since the root of Shabbat is this spiritual delight, which is da’at, through which all the severities drawn from the world of awe are raised and sweetened in the world of delight through the delights of Shabbat. Concerning this our Sages said, ‘And speak a word’: that your speech on Shabbat should not be like your weekday speech. For on Shabbat there is an ascent for speech, so that one speaks it with great delight through the da’at drawn down in the holiness of Shabbat; ‘and speak a word’ (ve-dabber davar), for ‘dabber’ is an expression of leading, and he leads the speech up to the world of delight. ... For what the Zohar says is known, that da’at is hidden in the mouth of the King; through speech one can raise and attain spiritual delight, by having da’at, and da’at is hidden and stored within speech. This is ‘to know that I am Hashem who sanctifies you’: to come through Shabbat to exalted da’at.”

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Tzav 5:1-2: “There are Torah scholars who are free only for Torah, toilers in Torah, as stated in the Ra’aya Meheimna (III 29b): Torah scholars, children of the King and Queen, are called Sabbaths. And there is one who does not merit so much and must engage in work for his food ... yet whenever he has free time he returns at once to his service and engages in Torah. These are called ‘those who grasp the Torah,’ for even in their work their intention is for the sake of Heaven, that they may fix times for Torah and raise their children to be Torah scholars, and they are called supporters of those who grasp the Torah. ... ‘And a son of man who holds fast to it’: that is, one who has not merited so much and must engage in work for his livelihood ... yet he is among those who grasp the Torah, for when he has free time he turns to words of Torah; and this requires guarding, lest he forget, Heaven forbid. Nevertheless, on Shabbat it is made entirely Torah, as stated at the beginning of Tanna DeVei Eliyahu; for even regarding laborers, who are very busy during the workdays ... the Pesikta applies the statement ‘Shabbatot were given only to engage in Torah’ to laborers. About this it says ‘a son of man who holds fast to it’: let him at least hold fast to the holiness of Shabbat, and then it will benefit him for the workdays, so that his intention in his work will be for the sake of Heaven, to raise his children to Torah study, and when he has free time on a week

k: volume-i|1926|0|R. Yehudah Aryeh Leib Alter, Sefat Emet,
quote: Parallel: R. Yehudah Aryeh Leib Alter, Sefat Emet, Chanukah 22:11: “Concerning the light that illuminates and the fire that burns, the holy Zohar says that on the workdays there is the luminary of fire and on Shabbat the luminaries of light; therefore on Motzaei Shabbat we make Havdalah with ‘Who creates the luminaries of fire,’ to join the luminary of fire to the luminaries of light of Shabbat (see there, Bereshit and Vayakhel). To explain the matter: there is a light that comes through burning the dross, for every lamp of ours gives light only according to what it has to consume and burn; and this is the purpose of all the labors of the workdays, to sort out and remove the dross, and through this sorting one merits light. But the illuminating light is the essence of light, which does not burn but only shines; it is the light created on the first day, which shone from one end of the world to the other, and the Holy One hid it away for the righteous. On Shabbat there is an illumination from the hidden light, as it says, ‘I have a good gift ...’; therefore it is called a gift, for it does not come through human action. And it is taught that after the first Shabbat, when the light was hidden, the Holy One prepared for man to find light by means of stone, and this is the aspect of the luminaries of fire, the burning fire: according to what one sorts, so one finds illumination.”

k: volume-i|1927|0|R. Chaim Tyrer of Czernowitz, Be'er Mayi
quote: Parallel: R. Chaim Tyrer of Czernowitz, Be'er Mayim Chaim, Shemot 10:1:17: “All this is what happened until now; but now, ‘Come unto Pharaoh,’ to warn him that from now on the three upper ones will be enclothed in order to strike him and crush his brain, with a new face from now, through the three upper ones that stand at the height of the world. And for this reason the Torah made such a great tumult over the redemption from Egypt, and we praise and rejoice over this redemption more than over all the redemptions and salvations with which Hashem saved His people Israel from all their foes, such as Sisera and Sennacherib and the like; for there was no such enclothing of the three upper ones against any of the ministering angels of the nations except in Egypt alone ... And therefore the author of the Haggadah arranged: ‘And I will pass through the land of Egypt: I and not an angel, I and not a seraph,’ etc., until ‘but the Holy One, blessed be He, in His glory and by Himself,’ until ‘I am Hashem: I am He and no other.’ ... It came only through the revelation of His glory, blessed be He, in the aspect of the light of the three upper ones.”

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Chodesh Adar 4: “For Pharaoh was Arich of the husk, as R. Chaim Vital of blessed memory wrote on what is in the holy Zohar (Bo 34a), ‘a certain supernal dragon ... the secret of the great dragon,’ that it is Arich of the husk. And then Israel were in Egypt like a fetus in its mother's womb ... that is, the husk surrounded Israel, and this was because the wisdom of Egypt then held sway and the wisdom of the Torah was there in exile. And Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, was a surrounding light, who surrounded Pharaoh with his wisdom, and through this he brought the wisdom of the Torah out from among them ... And so in the month of Adar is the erasing of Amalek, for the husk of Amalek is ‘the first of the nations,’ the beginning of the husk, like Pharaoh; only Pharaoh is Arich of the husk of lust, and Amalek is Arich of the husk of envy, anger and murder ... And the way of Amalek is that he can conceal himself so much that he misleads a person into calling evil good, and disguises himself as one who teaches him the good way, as in Chullin 91a: he appeared to him as a Torah scholar, as a rabbi showing the way.”

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Pekudei 3: “The main thing is that one be a Sabbath observer. Before the Giving of the Torah, He in His goodness renewed the work of Creation every day through the novel halakhah that the Holy One, blessed be He, innovates in the Heavenly Court each day, as stated in Bereishit Rabbah (49). This was so until Abraham our father, who fulfilled the entire Torah, Shabbat included, for he kept even eruv tavshilin, as stated in Yoma (28b) ... But the main purpose was that there be an Israelite nation that received the Torah, and then the novellae of halakhah were handed over to Israel, and they are called builders of the world, ‘builders’ who are engaged in the building of the world, as stated in Shabbat (114a).”

k: volume-i|1930|0|R. Shmuel Bornsztain of Sochatchov, Shem
quote: Parallel: R. Shmuel Bornsztain of Sochatchov, Shem MiShmuel, Purim 5: “My holy father, my master, of blessed memory, said that Shabbat has two aspects: a memorial of the work of Creation, as written in the First Tablets, and a remembrance of the Exodus from Egypt, as written in the Last Tablets. That is, just as at Creation it is written, ‘And He breathed into his nostrils the breath of life,’ so on Shabbat there is the extra soul; and just as at the Exodus there was the nullification and subjugation of the forces of matter, as explained in the Maharal, and as it is written, ‘Then the chiefs of Edom were terrified,’ and so on, so too Shabbat has the letters of boshet (shame), for matter is humbled. And Amalek is the reverse of Shabbat, for he was not moved and was not humbled.”

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Tetzaveh 6: “He was commanded ‘to work it and to guard it’: to work it with positive commandments and to guard it with negative commandments, as stated in the Zohar (I 27a). ... Everything was prepared for him so that he would have no distraction at all in the needs of his livelihood, for the fruits grew of themselves ... as it will be in the future ... Only after the sin was he told, ‘By the sweat of your brow you shall eat,’ ... and at the end of Kiddushin, ‘but I corrupted my deeds and forfeited my livelihood.’ Shabbat is to repair the sin of Adam, as we have said several times, and on Shabbat all Israel need not strive for the needs of their livelihood, for everything is prepared from Friday, and it is the day of rest. In the Yerushalmi (Shabbat 15) and the Pesikta (end of section 23): for laborers Shabbat was given only to engage in Torah, and for Torah scholars for delight, for we have no distraction at all, only to work it and guard it with positive and negative commandments. Guarding against desecrating Shabbat is the negative commandments, and the Torah and the Shabbat delight of the three meals are the positive commandments.”

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Vaera 9: “This Name was said to Jacob our father after he was called Israel, that is, that his bed was whole and would never again be spoiled. Then, before the birth of Benjamin, he was given the tidings, ‘A nation and a company of nations shall come from you,’ and it is stated in Bereishit Rabbah (82): your descendants are destined to make a nation like a company of peoples ... your descendants will offer sacrifices at a time when the high places are forbidden. One must understand why he was told then that Israel would offer sacrifices when the high places were forbidden. But at the birth of Benjamin ... Hashem announced that from his seed would come Elijah, who would offer sacrifice while the high places were forbidden ... so that through this all Israel would say, ‘Hashem, He is God.’ And it is stated in Vayikra Rabbah (31): ‘Your head upon you is like Carmel’: the empty ones among you are as dear to Me as Elijah who went up to Carmel. That is, the wicked, even though they spoiled much, Elijah the angel of the covenant will repair them, so that they are as dear as Elijah who sacrificed when the high places were forbidden. ... And he said, ‘and You turned their heart backward,’ for Hashem created the evil inclination ... so that there be light that issues from darkness, ... and Hashem conceded his words, as it is written, ‘and those whom I have harmed’ (Berakhot 32a).”

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Shemot 4: “Therefore the Arizal wrote that the time of these six weeks, the initials of Shovavim, is auspicious for repairing this blemish: from Shemot, in which the birth of Moses is mentioned, until Yitro, in which is the Giving of the Torah, when Israel went out from gloom to light. Afterward comes Mishpatim, in which it is written, ‘If you buy a Hebrew servant,’ and so on, that is, one who spoiled so much that he was sold as a servant, which this blemish causes. ... For the community as a whole the Egyptian exile accomplished this, that all of them were refined in the attribute of the Tzaddik ... yet an individual can still be one who spoils and must be sold as a servant to repair this blemish. About him it is written, ‘If you buy,’ and so on, ‘and in the seventh he shall go free,’ for he has repair in the aspect of the sabbatical year, the lower Sabbath. And even one who is sunk deepest, Heaven forbid, until he says, ‘I love my wife,’ and so on, even for him there is repair in the Jubilee, which is the aspect of the upper Sabbath. That is the great shofar, as it is written, ‘and those cast away in the land of Egypt shall come,’ that is, even those sunk in the husk of Egypt, the nakedness of the land: repentance will be awakened in their hearts through the great shofar.”

k: volume-i|1934|0|R. Chaim Tyrer of Czernowitz, Be’er Mayi
quote: Parallel: R. Chaim Tyrer of Czernowitz, Be’er Mayim Chaim, Acharei Mot (Leviticus 16:7): “The hairs, as is known, allude to the aspect of judgments, and the external forces take hold of them; therefore a Jew must always cast them off, especially on the eve of the holy Sabbath, when the light of Shabbat’s holiness is ready to come upon a person ... so that the external forces derive no benefit from the holiness. Perhaps this is what the verse says, ‘But against all (le-khol) the children of Israel no dog shall sharpen its tongue’: whoever among the children of Israel is in the aspect of Kol, whole in every completeness, with no trace of blemish at all, against him no dog shall sharpen its tongue at all. Not only can it not take hold of him to cleave to him and do him harm, Heaven forbid, but it must stand far from him and cannot bark at him at all ... And so Rashi explains on ‘And Joseph was of beautiful form’ that he curled his hair ... For in the blemish of that hair’s-breadth, Potiphar’s wife, the root of evil, found a place to provoke Joseph and entice him; without this curling she would have had no power to provoke him at all, since his source is blessed and there is no place of hold in him.”

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Pidyon HaBen 1: “At the plague of the firstborn it is written, ‘But against all the children of Israel no dog shall sharpen its tongue.’ Why would a dog sharpen its tongue? But the husk of the dog barks and prosecutes against the fact that the firstborn of Israel were then clarified as being in holiness, for Egypt is the husk of lust, and the main filth is in the firstborn. ... At the Giving of the Torah the filth ceased also from the cattle of Israel, as stated in Avodah Zarah (22b): the cattle of Israel are dear to them ... when the serpent came ... he cast filth into her ... Israel who stood at Mount Sinai, their filth ceased. And the meaning of ‘cast filth into her’ is the serpent’s venom, that is, to feel one’s own pleasure.”

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Vaera 14: “On Yom Kippur, it is stated (Yoma 20a), HaSatan has the numerical value of 364, and so on: on Yom Kippur he has no permission to accuse. Among the 364 days the Sabbaths are included as well, so that on Shabbat he does have permission to accuse. But at this meal we say, ‘Outside they remain and do not enter, these brazen dogs,’ that is, Amalek, who is the husk of the dog, as stated in the holy Zohar (II 65a), that he is a barking dog that accuses Israel. And in the Gemara, Megillah (13b): there was none who knew how to slander like Haman ... for all the accusations he spoke were meant to accuse them on high: ‘they sleep from the commandments,’ and the Rabbis are ‘one nation.’ This is the husk of Amalek, to accuse Israel; and at this meal they have no permission to accuse, as on Yom Kippur.”

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Ki Tavo 6: “The letter Samekh also carries an allusion of support for the fallen, for it alludes as well to ‘the secret (sod) of Hashem is with those who fear Him.’ It is like what we heard from our holy master of Izhbitz, of blessed memory, in the name of a certain master, concerning the plague of locusts: that the root of the creation of the locust is from the letter Samekh, and therefore the sound of their flight is ‘sa.’ That is, the root of every living creature that speaks is from all twenty-two letters of the Torah, and every animal has a special root in one letter, and the root of the locust is from the letter Samekh, which alludes to sod. Therefore it is said of this plague, ‘that you may tell in the ears of your son,’ for every plague was in the manner of ‘this opposite that,’ as the holy Zohar hints with ‘smiting and healing’: smiting for Egypt and healing for Israel. Just as they whispered in the opposite way, ‘they take crafty counsel (sod) against Your people,’ so through their being smitten by the plague of locusts, whose root is the letter Samekh, there came healing for Israel in the secret of ‘the sod of Hashem is with those who fear Him.’ ... And so the plague of locusts was the eighth of the ten plagues, which correspond to the ten attributes from below to above, and the plague of locusts corresponds to Binah of the heart, that is, that Binah enters the inner point of the heart, and through this the hidden one in the heart is subdued.

k: volume-i|1938|0|R. Chaim Tyrer of Czernowitz, Be'er Mayi
quote: Parallel: R. Chaim Tyrer of Czernowitz, Be'er Mayim Chaim, Shemot 10:1:21: “Further, Scripture says ‘that I may set these My signs ...’ until ‘what I have wrought upon Egypt, and My signs which I have set among them,’ and we must understand why ‘My signs’ is said twice. It is according to what the Arizal wrote in the intentions of the Pesach Seder, that arbeh, locust, alludes to the Name Ben, for four times ben (52) equals arbeh (208). ... Elohim is known to allude to Binah, from which judgments are aroused, and Ben alludes to Malchut; therefore this plague went forth from the Binah of the Malchut of holiness and struck the masculine Gevurah of the husk. ... And therefore it concludes, ‘and that you may tell in the ears of your son,’ for it is known what the Arizal wrote on the secret of the telling of the Exodus: that then the mouth of Ze'ir Anpin rose opposite the mouth of Tevunah, where the Yesod of the supernal Mother is, called ‘the mouth that speaks great things,’ and this is the secret of Pesach, peh sach, the mouth that speaks. Therefore, since it speaks here of the aspect of Binah, from which the plague of locusts went forth, it says ‘and that you may tell in the ears of your son,’ in which lies the secret of the telling of the Exodus.”

k: volume-i|1939|0|R. Kalonymus Kalman Epstein, Maor VaShem
quote: Parallel: R. Kalonymus Kalman Epstein, Maor VaShemesh, Vaera 15: “We have already written in the name of the Arizal that the plagues came upon them from below to above and from above to below, and the hail was from the sefirah of Chesed in holiness, and it struck the Netzach of the Other Side. And it is taught in the Kavanot on ‘and for the slanderers let there be no hope,’ that to execute judgments upon the enemies of Israel the attribute of Chesed too must consent to the judgments, and likewise to draw kindnesses upon the Congregation of Israel the attribute of judgment must consent. And this is what Rashi brings on ‘and there was hail, and fire flaring up,’ a miracle within a miracle, and the Midrash's parable of two hard legions at war with one another who made peace between them. Therefore the hail came from the attribute of Chesed, as above, for the attribute of Chesed too must agree with the attribute of judgment to take vengeance on the enemies of Israel ... ‘But the wheat (chitah) and the spelt (kusemet) were not smitten’: chitah has the numerical value of twenty-two, alluding to the twenty-two letters of the Torah, which is the plain meaning of the Torah; and kusemet alludes to the secrets of the Torah, from the word for covering. ‘They were not smitten, for they were late (afilot)’ alludes that revealed kindnesses and simple mercies were drawn upon Israel from the supernal Wonder (Pele), and this is ‘wonders of wonders were done for them.’”

k: volume-i|1940|0|R. Elimelech of Lizhensk, Noam Elimelech
quote: Parallel: R. Elimelech of Lizhensk, Noam Elimelech, Vayishlach 4: “It is taught in the Gemara: not like Abraham, who called the Temple a ‘mountain,’ ‘on the mountain Hashem will be seen,’ and not like Isaac, who called it a ‘field,’ ‘and Isaac went out to meditate in the field,’ but like Jacob, who called it a ‘house.’ ... The Patriarchs alluded to the First and Second Temples and to the future one, to be built speedily in our days. Abraham called it a mountain: this is the First Temple, when there were great righteous men who walked always in cleaving to Hashem ... and ‘mountain’ alludes to the upper worlds, of which there is no grasp except in thought and cleaving. ... And Isaac called it a field, that is, the Second Temple, when they were not righteous like the first ones and needed to make their repair on a lower level ... and this is ‘and Isaac went out to meditate (lasuach) in the field,’ sichah meaning speech ... And this is what Isaac said, ‘See, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a field’ ... Isaac our father wished to repair also in the bitter exile: if there will be such a righteous one who serves in cleaving, who is called a son to Hashem, he will have the power to repair the field ... and this is ‘see, the fragrance of my son,’ in the manner of the verse ‘the mandrakes give forth fragrance’: these are the youths of Israel who have not tasted the taste of sin.”

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Parshat Shekalim 6: “It is according to what is said in the holy Zohar (Bo 39b): ‘Whence did Isaac know the fragrance of a field which Hashem has blessed? Rather, they are two matters and all is one,’ for it is written, ‘And Isaac went out to meditate in the field’: that field was the one Abraham bought, adjacent to the cave ... In every place the site of the Temple is called a field, as in Pesachim 88a ... and the holy Zohar explains it of the Cave of Machpelah; and on this it says, ‘they are two matters and all is one.’ For Adam was created from the place of the altar ... and he should have been buried there as well, since he was taken from there, only that it was impossible to bury him there because of the impurity ... and he was buried in the Cave of Machpelah, and therefore it too has the holiness of the altar. ... The body was created in this world from the place of its atonement ... and after his passing the body can enter the Garden of Eden as well; the Cave of Machpelah is the gate to the Garden of Eden ... And this is ‘all is one’: the holiness of the Temple and of the Cave of Machpelah.”

Parallel: Resisei Layla 42:1: “Until the birth of Jacob and Esau, Isaac was engaged in distancing every kind of evil that is revealed, which people recognize as evil. But there are also those who call evil good, and so on, who to the eye can be imagined to be good while in truth they are the reverse. And this was Isaac’s test in sifting between Jacob and Esau, for Esau seemed better than Jacob in Isaac’s eyes. All of Isaac’s effort afterward was to clarify this recognition and to distance even the hidden evil, for in this lies the root of the name Israel, that is, a depth of good, the very opposite of Esau: although his outside is good, he is nonetheless evil, whereas in Israel, though their outside is evil, they are nonetheless good. This was Isaac’s whole labor, to bring forth a soul that would be so. Therefore, ‘He smelled the fragrance of his garments,’ and the Sages said (Sanhedrin 37a), ‘the fragrance of his betrayers,’ ‘and he blessed him,’ for the recognition of completeness comes precisely through the fragrance of his betrayers, that his bed is whole.”

k: volume-i|1943|0|Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the F
ref: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12:1
quote: Parallel: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 12:1: “It is known that there are three levels in apprehending Hashem, blessed be He: ‘I,’ ‘You,’ and ‘He,’ which are like the branches of the tree, the trunk, and the roots in the ground. ‘I’ is the meal of the field of holy apples, on Shabbat night, as it is written in Bereishit Rabbah (65:22) on the verse ‘as the fragrance of a field which Hashem has blessed’ (Genesis 27:27): this is a field of apples. And this is ‘the fragrance of his betrayers’ (there), that even the sins of the children of Israel give off a good fragrance. And this is the holiness of Shabbat upon the six days of work: on what has already passed, Shabbat bestows holiness, declaring that all of it was for the sake of Heaven and good.”

k: volume-i|1944|0|R. Shmuel Bornsztain of Sochatchov, Shem
quote: Parallel: R. Shmuel Bornsztain of Sochatchov, Shem MiShmuel, Purim 9: “In the Talmud, Ta’anit (15a): Not all are destined for light, and not all for gladness, but the righteous for light and the upright for gladness, as it is written, ‘Light is sown for the righteous, and gladness for the upright of heart.’ Rashi explains that the upright are superior to the righteous. It seems the meaning is this: a tzaddik is one to whom a deed came and he overpowered his inclination and was saved, like Yosef the Tzaddik; but the upright are those in whom every crookedness has been straightened, who have turned darkness into light and bitterness into sweetness. Therefore, just as the tzaddik pushed his inclination away from himself, so he merits light, to illuminate the darkness, but the darkness still exists. The upright, however, merit gladness as well, for it is written, ‘Strength and joy are in His place,’ and the absence of joy comes from the external forces; when the spirit of impurity is removed from the land, then joy will reach its completion in the world. ... Therefore the upright, who have turned the evil within them to good, merit true gladness.”

k: volume-i|1945|0|R. Moshe Chaim Ephraim of Sudilkov, Dege
quote: Parallel: R. Moshe Chaim Ephraim of Sudilkov, Degel Machaneh Ephraim, Bo 8: “Or one may say, ‘And all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings’: it is known that one who cleaves to truth cleaves to light, for ‘in the light of the King’s face is life,’ unlike one who is in falsehood, a denier (makhchish), which is a permutation of choshekh, darkness. And this is what struck the Egyptians, that they had thick darkness, while Israel had light. ... For the Egyptians, who cleaved to denial, there was made for them the permutation of darkness and gloom. And this is ‘no man rose from his place’: certainly, when one cleaves to falsehood and darkness and gloom rule over him, that is a great fall and he cannot rise; and the reverse, through light it is said, ‘Arise, shine, for your light has come,’ and then you can rise. ‘For behold, darkness shall cover the earth’: what is darkness comes from the fact that ‘it covers the earth,’ that is, truth, as in ‘truth springs from the earth,’ meaning that truth was covered from them and not revealed in them, since they cleave only to falsehood and denial; from this, darkness is drawn.”

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Pesach 46:1: “The first utterance, Bereishit, is the concealed intellect beyond all thought, and there are mentioned the darkness and the tohu va-vohu, which allude to the deeds of the wicked (Bereishit Rabbah 2). Then it becomes clear that the sins of Israel are ‘like these years’ (shanim) that are arranged and come from the six days of Creation (Shabbat 89b); that is, this was the order of the world’s creation, first darkness and then light (there, 77b), so that there should be light that issues from darkness and good that issues from evil, that it be ‘very good’ (Zohar II 184a). Then ‘they shall become white as snow,’ for deliberate sins become like merits. This is not so for the idolaters, who are the darkness, the tohu and the vohu that allude to the four kingdoms; they are actual darkness. ... In Israel, their darkness is the light that issues from darkness, which is the main intent of the utterance Bereishit. ... And this is as it says (Sanhedrin 99a): ‘When does the Messiah come?’ ... ‘For behold, darkness shall cover the earth ... but upon you Hashem shall shine,’ and as it says in the plague of darkness, ‘and all the children of Israel had light.’”

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Tzav 4:1: “It is stated in the Midrash (Tanchuma, beginning of Noach) that the wicked are judged in Gehenna only with darkness, and so it is in Shemot Rabbah (14): ‘This tub, with what is it covered? With an earthen vessel. So too the wicked,’ etc., ‘and darkness was on the face of the deep: this is Gehenna,’ etc. ... But the darkness is only for the idolaters, and it is fire, ‘and given over to the burning fire.’ In Israel, even the sinners of Israel who descend to Gehenna, it is stated in the Gemara (Eruvin 19a) that they weep and shed tears like the spring of the Shittin, and justify the judgment upon themselves, and through this they extinguish the fire of Gehenna, and from the fire there is made for them the light of Gehenna.”

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Tazria 2:1: “The roots of the husks are seven, corresponding to the seven lower attributes in holiness, ‘one opposite the other God made’ ... and opposite them are the seven nations, whose root is the Canaanite, the Hittite and the Amorite. These correspond to the heads of the husks, which are envy, lust and honor, and these stand against the holiness of the Patriarchs, who are the reverse of these three traits. Abraham our father, who loved people, is the reverse of the husk of envy, the husk of Esau, who hates blood that is not in his own body (Bereishit Rabbah 63). Isaac our father, whose trait was dread and awe, is the reverse of the husk of lust, the husk of Ishmael. And Jacob our father, who was lowly in his own eyes and said, ‘I am too small,’ stands against the husk of arrogance and honor, the husk of Amalek ... And so our holy master the Rebbe of Lublin reckoned (in his book, Lech Lecha): the Canaanite against the attribute of Chesed in holiness, the Hittite, from chatat (terror), against the attribute of awe in holiness, and the Amorite against the attribute of Tiferet ... These three nations are the three husks of envy, lust and honor, which are the reverse of the life of the Patriarchs’ holiness.”

k: volume-i|1949|0|R. Yehudah Aryeh Leib Alter, Sefat Emet,
quote: Parallel: R. Yehudah Aryeh Leib Alter, Sefat Emet, Bo 23: “In the Midrash on ‘And you shall take a bunch of hyssop’: ‘I make you into one bunch for Myself; even though you are lowly like hyssop, in the merit of the Patriarchs,’ and so on. For this was the essence of the redemption: to be drawn after the deeds of the Patriarchs. Children truly are drawn after the deeds of their fathers, but they had become mixed among the nations, and so the attachment to the root was severed; and this was the redemption, to become one bunch and to be separated from the mixture. Therefore, ‘and you shall reach (ve-higatem) the lintel ... the two side-posts,’ as explained elsewhere, that this is what the Sages said: a person must say, ‘When will my deeds reach (yagi’u) the deeds of my fathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob?’ And they merited this at the Exodus without gradual progression, and about this it is written, ‘leaping over the mountains’ in the merit of the Patriarchs, for the Holy One, blessed be He, raised them to cleave to the deeds of the Patriarchs.”

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Yitro 11: “And in the Mishnah, Avot chapter 3: ‘Reflect upon three things and you will not come to sin: from where you came, from a putrid drop; and where you are going,’ and so on; ‘and before Whom you are destined to give judgment,’ and so on. ... It may be said that this is the meaning of what is said in Sotah (5a): basar (flesh) is bushah (shame), seruchah (putrid), rimah (worm). ... And this is what is said, ‘And it shall come to pass that from Sabbath to Sabbath all flesh shall come,’ and so on. According to what is expounded at the beginning of Seder Eliyahu Rabbah, ‘Where is the place of My rest,’ refers to Shabbat, and it is written, ‘But to this one will I look, to the poor and contrite of spirit, who trembles at My word.’ On Shabbat, when a person reflects on all that passed over him in the days of work, he becomes poor and contrite of spirit and trembling at the word of Hashem. This corresponds to these three things: by taking to heart that he comes from a putrid drop, he is poor at his root, without strength; contrite of spirit, when he thinks of his end, that he goes to a place of dust and so on; and trembling at the word of Hashem, when he thinks that he is destined to give judgment and reckoning before the King of kings, and dread and shame of Hashem fall upon him.”

k: volume-i|1951|0|R. Yehudah Aryeh Leib Alter, Sefat Emet,
quote: Parallel: R. Yehudah Aryeh Leib Alter, Sefat Emet, Vayetzei 20 (5652): “It is stated in the Gemara: whoever delights in the Sabbath is given an inheritance without boundaries, ‘and I will feed you the inheritance of Jacob your father,’ ‘and you shall spread out west and east.’ The matter is as it is written, ‘The land on which you lie,’ that the Holy One, blessed be He, folded up the entire Land of Israel, and so on. This is the root point, the Foundation Stone, which is the root of the whole world; and Jacob our father, the complete man for whose sake all was created, merited the place of the foundation on which everything depends. And it is written, ‘To you I will give it, and to your seed,’ so every Jew too has a share in this gift. This is fulfilled on the holy Sabbath, as the Sages said, ‘I have a good gift in My treasure house, and Shabbat is its name.’ Therefore it is written of Shabbat, ‘Let no man go out of his place,’ from which it follows that Shabbat gives every Jew a place. ... And just as it is said of Jacob that Mount Moriah leapt toward him, so too, precisely, is the extra soul given to Israel on Shabbat, and about this it is said, ‘Who spreads the shelter of peace over us ... and over Jerusalem.’”

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Behar 14: “Israel on Shabbat are as in the Sanctuary, for Shabbat in time is like the Sanctuary in place, as explained several times; and just as in the Sanctuary dread and awe fall upon whoever enters it, so on Shabbat, upon every one of Israel, as in the Sanctuary, falls dread and awe, as it is written, ‘with great awe’: this is the revelation of the Shechinah. And so we say in the song of Shabbat, ‘Planted in the house of Hashem, they shall flourish in the courtyards of our God.’ ... And even one who is not a Torah scholar, on Shabbat every one of Israel is in the courtyards of the house of Hashem, for the dread of Shabbat is upon the unlearned, and on Shabbat all Israel are like Torah scholars.”

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Shabbat HaGadol 10: “Although they had not yet been commanded concerning Shabbat, nevertheless the holiness of Shabbat is fixed and enduring from the side of Hashem, blessed be He, as stated in Pesachim (117b), for Hashem Himself called Shabbat holy, as it is said, ‘and He sanctified it.’ And the whole power by which Israel sanctify the festivals comes through the holiness of Shabbat that Israel merit, and through it they are able to make a ‘holy convocation.’ Pesach was the first that Israel sanctified, and this is what we say, ‘First of the holy convocations, a remembrance of the Exodus from Egypt.’ ... And the power Israel had to call Pesach holy at the Exodus, when it was taken on the tenth, also came through the holiness of Shabbat, which fell then on Shabbat, as stated. Moses called it the Great Shabbat, for the holiness of Shabbat caused Israel to be able to call things holy.”

k: volume-i|1954|0|R. Shmuel Bornsztain of Sochatchov, Shem
quote: Parallel: R. Shmuel Bornsztain of Sochatchov, Shem MiShmuel, Ha’azinu 1: “It seems that it was good news for Israel that even someone as low and lacking as this is alluded to in the Torah, as we explained on the verse in Parashat Bo, ‘And it shall come to pass, when your children say to you, What is this service to you?’ The passage ends, ‘And the people bowed and prostrated themselves,’ and Rashi explains: over the tidings of children. At first glance this is hard to understand, for it speaks of the wicked son who said, ‘What is this service to you?’ And in Midrash Rabbah (Lech Lecha 42:9), Abraham said, ‘And I go childless: if I am destined to raise sons who will anger You, better that I go childless.’ If so, what good tiding is this? But it may be said that this is the tiding: that even their wicked son is alluded to in the Torah, and since the Torah is eternal, he has a hold and a root in eternity, and through this, in the end, after causes and turnings, he will be purified and made white, for ‘no castaway will be banished from Him.’ And this itself is the tiding alluded to in this passage.”

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Vayechi 17: “After Havdalah. The Sages said (Shevuot 18b): whoever makes Havdalah over wine at the departure of Sabbaths will have male children ... children fit to issue rulings, as it is written, ‘to distinguish and to teach.’ One must understand what the obligation to make Havdalah over wine is. Granted that Kiddush, which is in the joy of Shabbat’s entry, requires wine, as it says, ‘wine gladdens’; but Havdalah at the departure of Shabbat, ‘of joy, what does it accomplish?’ ... On the surface there is no perceptible distinction to sense between the holiness of Shabbat and the six workdays, except for one to whom Hashem has granted a portion of understanding (binah) ... That is, precisely at the Havdalah of Saturday night, if he senses in his soul, with a fine discernment of the heart’s understanding, that the time has changed from holy to profane, like ‘from a high roof,’ and so on, for then precisely he has the feeling and longing for the holiness of Shabbat. This is ‘whoever makes Havdalah over wine on Saturday night’: he has joy from sensing the holiness of Shabbat at the moment of its parting, through the discernment of his mind (da’at). He merits children fit to issue rulings, measure for measure, for ruling is likewise a fine discernment of the mind, to distinguish between impure and pure.”

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Devarim 17: “‘Give ... wine to the bitter of soul,’ as it is written, ‘and wine gladdens the heart of enosh,’ that is, even one at the level of enosh, which is a lower level, as they expounded (Shabbat 118b) on ‘Happy is the enosh who does this’: even if he served idols like the generation of Enosh, he is forgiven. That is, after Shabbat passes and the workdays come, a person is very bitter of soul, as I heard from our holy master, of blessed memory, who said in the name of one: at the departure of Shabbat it is as though one is cast ‘from a high roof to a deep pit.’ For this reason we say on Saturday night the verse, ‘Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust and not fear,’ and one says ‘do not fear’ only to one who is afraid, for then dread falls on a person when he sees that he is leaving the holiness of Shabbat for the weekdays. Therefore we say, ‘I will trust in my salvation and not fear,’ and for this reason we also say the Psalm against afflictions on Saturday night.”

k: volume-i|1957|0|R. Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev, Kedushat
quote: Parallel: R. Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev, Kedushat Levi, Beshalach: “Ramban wrote that it is a mitzvah to mention the Sabbath day on every day of the week: on the first day one says, ‘Today is the first day in the Sabbath,’ and so on all the days of the week, and he wrote that this is the plain meaning of ‘Remember the Sabbath day to sanctify it’: to remember Shabbat every day ... The effect is that by remembering Shabbat every day, he looks forward every day to the Sabbath day, to keep it; then when Shabbat arrives he will guard it as is fitting, without desecrating it, Heaven forbid, since it is dear to him, having awaited it. ... This explains the verse, ‘How long will you refuse to keep (lishmor)’: it says ‘to keep’ because shamor is a term of waiting, as in ‘and his father kept (shamar) the matter,’ which means looking forward and hoping for the thing, when will it come to his hand.”

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Vaetchanan 21:1: “As it is written, ‘For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, says Hashem, thoughts of peace and not of evil, to give you a future and a hope.’ ‘A future’ (acharit) means that the good is seen openly, like what is said (Bava Batra 14b) of Ruth, ‘a tribulation that has a future,’ for they saw that David came from it. So too, immediately in the Babylonian exile they saw that the Oral Torah spread through the Men of the Great Assembly ... and as it says (Sukkah 20a), ‘Ezra came up from Babylonia and established it.’ This is the meaning of ‘future,’ and it is what is expounded (Ta’anit 29b), ‘these are date-palms and linen garments,’ which hint at the Oral Torah, for in Babylonia there were date-palms, ... and the linen garments are what is said (Kiddushin 72a), that the scholars of Babylonia resemble the ministering angels. And our holy teacher said that ‘acharit’ denotes the Oral Torah, which is the last attribute, Malkhut, ‘the mouth, which we call the Oral Torah’; and it hints at date-palms, which is the last of the seven species. ‘And hope’ refers to the future, for I heard from our holy teacher, who said in the name of R. Bunim, that although the minds diminish with each generation, the point of life in the heart keeps widening and becomes more refined each time in exile.”

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Beshalach 12:1: “Afterward it is written, ‘They could not drink the waters of Marah,’ and their souls were bitter within them that they could not drink water, ‘for they were bitter.’ There are words of Torah that are called ‘still waters,’ from which one attains rest in the heart, and there are words of Torah from which bitterness comes into the heart, as in the holy Zohar (III 229b and 153a), and as the Gemara (Shabbat 87a) expounds on the word va-yaged: things that draw a person’s heart like aggadah, and things that are hard for a person like sinews. On this it is written, ‘and Hashem showed him (va-yorehu) a tree,’ which the Targum renders ‘and He taught him.’ This is what is said in Midrash Rabbah (Vayakhel 50): the generation was bitter in its deeds, and therefore the waters, which are words of Torah, were bitter to them, turned to bitterness for them. ‘And Hashem showed him’: He taught him His ways, that the Holy One, blessed be He, heals the bitter with the bitter, as in Midrash Rabbah 23. And this follows what is said in the holy Zohar (II 184a): there is no light except that which comes out of darkness, and good that comes out of evil becomes ‘very good.’”

k: volume-i|1960|0|R. Chaim Tyrer of Chernowitz, Sidduro Sh
ref: Sidduro Shel Shabbat, Volume II, Derush III 2:17
quote: Parallel: R. Chaim Tyrer of Chernowitz, Sidduro Shel Shabbat, Derush 3, 2:17: “First it spoke of the aspect of sufferings that come upon people, and said, ‘They came to Marah and could not drink the waters of Marah’; afterward it said, ‘There He made for them a statute and an ordinance,’ which is the aspect of the judgments that reach one who transgresses His will. ... Then, after you accept the sufferings with love, I promise you first of all: ‘All the sickness that I placed upon Egypt,’ to harden the heart of Pharaoh and his servants so that they would not repent through the sufferings, and therefore I struck them blow after blow, this I will not place upon you. And further it said that your reward is with you in two aspects. One, ‘for I am Hashem,’ faithful to pay reward, ... hints at the first two aspects, that the sufferings come to increase one’s reward in the World to Come. The second, ‘your Healer,’ hints at the two latter aspects, which come in the likeness of healing: just as one heals a person with bitter drugs and with bloodletting, so are the sufferings sent, so that through them the soul will be healed.”

k: volume-i|1961|0|R. Yehudah Aryeh Leib Alter, Sefat Emet,
quote: Parallel: R. Yehudah Aryeh Leib Alter, Sefat Emet, Ki Tisa 10:2: “Shabbat depends on the days of action, and whenever Israel rectified the realm of action, Shabbat was given to them: at Mount Sinai, which was the rectification of the forty-two (as it is said, ‘which was made at Mount Sinai’), Shabbat was given to them; and after the sin, when they spoiled the ‘we will do,’ and it was rectified afterward through the making of the Mishkan, the mitzvah of Shabbat returned to them. … Now of the first Tablets it is said, ‘the work of God were they’: that is, they were the root of action, in which there is an aspect of Godliness. Therefore the Sages said that the Tablets were created on the eve of Shabbat at twilight, and this is the cleaving of action to the day of Shabbat, which is the soul. Of the last ones it is said, ‘Hew for yourself … like the first.’ One may wonder how there could be in this world something like the first, of which it is said ‘the work of God were they.’ It seems that in truth they are the first and they are the last, only the first needed no refining and therefore were in the open, for there was no evil in the world at all, as it says ‘freedom’ (charut); only afterward, when it is written ‘and he broke them,’ it became necessary to refine the good from the mixture of dross, and as the righteous continually refine, so the power of the Torah is renewed.”

Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Tetzaveh 5:1: “Afterward, when they said, ‘You speak with us and we will listen,’ the evil inclination returned to its place; and after the spoiling, it was said to Moses our teacher, ‘Hew for yourself two tablets of stone’: that from now on, since their heart had become a heart of stone, it was necessary to hew the stone tablets through human action, meaning that through a person’s toil in Torah he will merit from now on that the words of Torah be engraved even upon the heart of stone. … This is what they alluded to (Avot 5) when they counted among the ten things created on the eve of Shabbat at twilight ‘the writing, the engraving tool, and the Tablets.’ The engraving tool (michtav) is the stylus that engraves upon stone; that is, the preparation, through a person’s toil in words of Torah, for them to be absorbed in the heart so as to rectify even the heart of stone. … They said (Nedarim 22b), ‘Had Israel not sinned, only the five books of the Torah would have been given to them,’ and so forth, for ‘in much wisdom is much anger’: to rectify the much anger, so that the words of Torah be engraved upon a heart of stone, much wisdom is needed.”

k: volume-i|1963|0|R. Tzvi Elimelech Shapira of Dinov, Bnei
quote: Parallel: R. Tzvi Elimelech Shapira of Dinov, Bnei Yissaschar, Adar 3:4:3-4: “Second introduction: you know the Sages’ saying that although the four death penalties of the court have ceased, the law of the four death penalties has not ceased. So it was even in the time of the Sanhedrin: one who did not receive his punishment through the Sanhedrin, for example because there were no witnesses or they found some merit for him, his punishment was not given into their hands; but He who knows hidden things knows and is witness, and if he did not repent, He brings about for him the death fitting for him to receive his punishment according to the Torah.
